history.heading: Bohemia and Moravia
paragraphs: The Czech lands take their Latin name, Bohemia, from the Celtic Boii tribe. Slavs settled there in the 6th century, and Great Moravia, a Slavic state of the 9th century, received the missionaries Cyril and Methodius. The Přemyslid dynasty founded the Duchy, later Kingdom, of Bohemia, with Saint Wenceslas as its patron saint.
Under Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor and King of Bohemia, Prague became one of Europe's greatest cities in the 14th century; he founded Charles University in 1348 and built the Charles Bridge.

history.heading: Reformation and Habsburg rule
paragraphs: The church reformer Jan Hus was burned at the stake in 1415, sparking the Hussite Wars. Bohemia came under the Habsburgs in 1526. The Defenestration of Prague in 1618 began the Thirty Years' War, and after the Protestant defeat at the Battle of White Mountain in 1620, the Czech lands were re-Catholicised and Germanised.
The Czech National Revival of the 19th century restored the Czech language and culture.

history.heading: Czechoslovakia
paragraphs: Czechoslovakia was founded on 28 October 1918 under Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk and became a prosperous democracy between the wars. The 1938 Munich Agreement forced it to cede the Sudetenland to Nazi Germany, which occupied the rest in 1939. Most Czech Jews were murdered in the Holocaust. After the war, about three million Germans were expelled.

Communists took power in 1948. The Prague Spring reforms of 1968, under Alexander Dubček, were crushed by a Warsaw Pact invasion. The peaceful Velvet Revolution of 1989, led by dissidents including the playwright Václav Havel, ended communism.

history.heading: Czech Republic
paragraphs: Czechoslovakia peacefully split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993, the "Velvet Divorce". The Czech Republic joined NATO in 1999 and the European Union in 2004. It adopted the short name Czechia in 2016.

culture.heading: Literature, music and film
paragraphs: Czech is a West Slavic language. Writers include Franz Kafka, who wrote in German in Prague, Jaroslav Hašek (The Good Soldier Švejk), Karel Čapek, who coined the word "robot", and Milan Kundera. Composers include Antonín Dvořák, Bedřich Smetana and Leoš Janáček.
Czech cinema includes the Oscar-winning films of the Czechoslovak New Wave, and Czech animation and puppetry have a strong tradition.

culture.heading: Beer and traditions
paragraphs: Czechs drink more beer per person than any other nation, and Pilsner lager was invented in Plzeň in 1842. Food includes roast pork with dumplings and sauerkraut, svíčková and trdelník pastries.
Czechia is one of the least religious countries in the world. Prague's historic centre and Český Krumlov are UNESCO sites. Ice hockey is the most popular sport, along with football and tennis.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Czechia is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the government, responsible to the Chamber of Deputies, while the directly elected president has a mainly representative role but some important powers, including appointing the prime minister. Parliament also has a Senate.
Andrej Babiš's populist ANO movement won the 2025 parliamentary election and returned to government. Czechia is a member of the EU and NATO and has been a strong supporter of Ukraine.

economy.heading: Industrial economy
paragraphs: Czechia is one of the most prosperous post-communist countries, with a strong industrial base. Car manufacturing is central, led by Škoda (part of Volkswagen), along with machinery, electronics, glass and beer. Its economy is closely integrated with Germany's.
Czechia has low unemployment and relatively low inequality. It has kept the Czech koruna rather than adopting the euro. Challenges include high energy costs and dependence on the automotive industry.
